transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-05 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Laura Kim (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (Argosy CTO), Evan Ruiz (Argosy SRE), Priya Narayan (Argosy ML Eng)

Summary (auto): Quick bench readout and routing triage vs incumbent, focused on tail latency under burst.

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we got 42 minutes on the calendar, quick intros... Maya, Evan, Priya, thanks for carving out time.
[00:14] Maya: Thanks Samir, good to see you. We want to get through the delta numbers vs our baseline and decide whether to push for a dedicated slot.
[00:23] Laura: Cool, we'll go through the lab runs. Quick note: some of the metric names in our dashboard might look slightly different than yours, like p95 we call 95th percentile but same idea.
[00:36] Evan: that's fine, just want to call out the big one — during bursts we saw p99 spikes that the incumbent didn't show.
[00:44] Laura: right, so first slide — run 1 at steady concurrency 50 QPS. Redwood p50~80ms, p95~210ms, p99~360ms. Baseline p95 reported 220ms, p99~300ms. So p95 is actually slightly better on our side, p99 a touch higher.
[01:08] Priya: are those with KT cache on? we turned on the prefix caching in our harness.
[01:15] Laura: yes, we enabled KV cache in these runs but note our cache hit rate for that particular workload was only 42% — because there's a lot of unique prompts.
[01:25] Maya: ok, interesting. Where do you think the p99 delta comes from? is it GPU scheduling, queueing, or network?
[01:33] Laura: From traces it's a mix — short-lived queueing when bursts hit a shard boundary, and occasional longer decode steps when attention pattern length spikes. Also we caught a routing fallback on run 3 where requests spilled to a lower-capacity node — that added tail time.
[01:52] Evan: can you clarify fallback? we thought fallbacks were immediate but our infra shows a retry loop.
[01:58] Samir: yeah that's a good point — we have a policy that will try primary node then fallback variant once, but if the fallback is a smaller quantized model it may be slower for certain long-context requests. We can tune that to prefer same-capacity variants.
[02:17] Priya: That could explain it. A smaller quantized model increases token time in our tests sometimes. Do you have logs we can inspect?
[02:23] Laura: we'll share the routing traces — the ones that show per-hop latency. I'll compress and put them in the shared drive.
[02:31] Maya: Another question: throughput plateau — in run 4 at 200 concurrent connections we saw throughput flattening and overall tail latency jump. Is there a batching config we can change?
[02:42] Laura: yes, two levers: increase batch size ceiling for that worker pool, or enable adaptive batching which will briefly favor throughput over latency. For argosy use-case, if you need consistent p95 under 300ms we recommend adaptive batching with conservative timeouts.
[02:58] Evan: what's the cost delta for that? we can't blow up token costs.
[03:03] Samir: adaptive batching trades a little latency for token efficiency — actually can reduce compute per token in high-volume cases, so cost per token may go down but per-request latency mixing will vary. We'll model costs on your 2M monthly tokens once you provide the trace.
[03:20] Priya: about quantization — you mentioned a 4-bit quant profile for the fallback. How much accuracy drop did you see on our eval prompts?
[03:28] Laura: For the tuning runs we compared outputs on your eval suite — ROUGE-ish metrics show minor diffs, about 1-2% drop in our automatic metric for certain long context summaries. Human review might flag style changes but not factual errors in most samples.
[03:44] Maya: so maybe keep the primary as FP16 or 8-bit and only fallback to 4-bit when capacity is exhausted?
[03:51] Samir: exactly, that's our suggested routing policy — prefer same-precision variants, fallback to quantized models only after retry threshold.
[03:58] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[04:03] Evan: about the dedicated slot — what's in scope? is it full isolation or shared GPU with reservations?
[04:10] Samir: Dedicated means reserved GPU pool with pinning for your tenant, and we can guarantee throughput SLOs per slot. For pilots we can allocate a 'reserved pool' but not full bare-metal isolated racks unless we move to Private.
[04:26] Priya: That might be enough. For the pilot we just need predictable p99 and a way to reproduce the spikes.
[04:33] Laura: we'll provision a 4-GPU reserved pool for two weeks and run your mixed-trace. That should surface whether queueing is the culprit.
[04:41] Maya: perfect. Timelines?
[04:44] Samir: we can stand up the slot by 2027-10-07. Laura will need the workload trace and an allowlist for the trial IPs.
[04:54] Priya: I'll send the trace today, but need to scrub PII — it's synthetic.
[05:00] Maya: also security — what's the compliance posture? do you provide audit logs and KMS integration?
[05:08] Samir: yes, we do KMS and encryption at rest, plus per-request audit logs retained per contract. For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS. We'll share SOC2/ISO docs in the drive.
[05:21] Evan: great. One last technical note — can you expose detailed per-token latency breakdowns? we want to correlate slow decodes to token position.
[05:30] Laura: we can — our traces include per-token timing with model stage tags, though it's a lot of data. We'll deliver compressed CSVs with sample slices.
[05:40] Priya: that'll help.
[05:44] Samir: Alright, to recap: Redwood to provision 2-week dedicated trial starting 10/07; Argosy to share scrubbed workload trace and allowlist; Laura to share routing traces and p95/p99 logs; Samir to loop in billing/security contacts and share the trial contract.
[06:02] Maya: sounds good.
[06:05] Laura: any blockers on our side? none.
[06:08] Evan: nope.
[06:10] Samir: we'll also model cost delta and send a short spreadsheet by 10/12.
[06:16] Maya: ok thanks everyone.
[06:20] Laura: thanks, talk soon.
[06:23] [meeting end]
